replying_to: Replying to Mutual Information Estimation as a Difference of Entropies for Unsupervised Representation Learning
display_title: Official Review of Paper3965 by Reviewer 6s5e

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes a new loss for an already exiting framework of self-supervised learning. A classical formulation of a self supervised learning is used here and illustrated in Figure 1. Two views of the same image are created and propagated through a feature network and MLP head and the corresponding features are further normalized. The proposed solution suggests to maximize the mutual information of the features that correspond to the two views of an image. The paper derives this mutual information using Neuman Entropy (which estimation is claimed to be more stable. compared to Shannon entropy, when small batch size is used). The estimation of the Neuman Entropy suggested by the authors is summarized in the PyTorch pseudo code in Algorithm 1. Throughout the paper the authors emphasize that the derived approximations for entropy and conditional entropy (sections 5.1 and 5.2) only hold for a weak Gaussian noise augmentation.
The authors illustrate that the method can be effectively used even with relatively small batch sizes (Figure 3 )
The authors illustrate the effectiveness of their method comparing it to other state of the art self-supervised  approaches in Tables 1 and 2 and achieve SOTA performance in transfer learning task for COCO.
content.main_review:
Strengths of the paper:
1. It is always interesting to see how fundamental theories (e.g. quantum mechanics in this case) can be useful in relatively experimental field, such as deep learning for Computer Vision. The authors provide such an opportunity, outlining basics of quantum mechanics to explain the suggested estimation of the mutual entropy using Neuman  Entropy. In overall, it was interesting to learn how familiar cosine similarity can be interpreted as an approximation of a conditional entropy.   
2. Beyond extensive theoretical derivations the authors provide basic experiments, which illustrate effectiveness of trained features on ImageNet classification task and transfer learning for Object Detection on COCO and PascalVOC benchmarks. The suggested method even achieves SOTA for Coco detection benchmark.

Weakness:
1. As much as it was interesting to refresh the memory of the basics of quantum mechanics (provided in Section 3), this review does not contribute to the paper in overall. The explanation about <braket> does not really add intuition or understanding of the further proofs. The only mention of  "braket" notation in the definition related to the final estimations appears in Definition 3.1 of the density operator. Instead of the elaborated presentation of the quantum mechanics basics, I would suggest the authors to provide more intuition (and maybe theory) on why their approximation based on Neuman Entropy allows to use smaller batch size compared to Shannon entropy. Another option would be to include the training details in the main text (instead of supplementary) 
2. Figure 2 is not clear to me, specifically, what is presented in the y axis - is it as stated - mutual information in (a) and entropy in (b) and (c) -  why would we like to compare mutual information with entropy? Also it is not clear if in this experiment the authors base their implementation of Shannon entropy on anything previously reported in the literature with respect to self-supervised learning. Previously, they say that typically contrastive learning is based on Shannon entropy, but then it is not clear why it fails in the experiment presented in Figure 2 (Variance analysis), while being successful as part of Sim-SIAM (Table 2 (b))
3. It is concerning that different data augmentation policy is implied with the proposed approach, compared to Sim-SIAM (Table 5) -- it might happen that the observed difference in the performance actually comes from this different policy and not from the loss. It could have been helpful to see performance of the suggested method with the exact same augmentation policy.
4. It would be helpful to have some discussion on difference in performance between Pascal VOC and COCO. Why are the learned representations more effective for COCO (at least with respect to other methods)? 
5. Finally the suggested loss is not symmetric with respect to the two views and this is very counter-intuitive. Why is not the loss calculated twice permuting the two views and summed? In other words, I would expect the following formulation for the loss in Algorithm1 :  
Loss = (eig val(U1)*log(eig val(U1))).sum()  + (eig val(U2)*log(eig val(U2))).sum() - 2* beta * cosine_similairty (U1, U2) .mean()
content.summary_of_the_review: I tend to weakly accept this paper, as it contributes a new loss that has an interesting theoretical background. The experiments are not strikingly impressive however: Sim-SIAM tends to perform equally well for batch size -128 (Table 2 b) and it is not clear why the learned features are effective for COCO but not for Pascal VOC (Table 3). Also the assumption of weak Gaussian noise augmentation is somewhat limiting the validity of the entire theoretical derivation, given that it was shown that diverse augmentation is a key for self-supervised learning success (and also given that the actual experiments are performed with other types of augmentations - Tables 4 & 5)
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

display_title: Official Review of Paper3965 by Reviewer g1dt

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a method for unsupervised representation learning based on mutual information estimation that does not involve a contrastive loss and therefore does not need a large batch size to be trained. This is achieved by estimation of the mutual information with the difference of von Neumann entropies as a bound for the Shannon entropies.
content.main_review:
Strong points:
1. The principled approach for representation learning based on the mutual information estimation
2. What seems to be a novel idea to use the von Neumann entropy for mutual information estimation rather than the Shannon entropy
3. The novel approach for the mutual information estimation avoids using the contrastive loss and therefore does not have to have a large batch size - a huge limitation of the methods based on the contrastive loss
4. State-of-the-art performance demonstrated on image datasets

Weak points:
1. Loose mathematical derivation (see details below)
2. (minor due to understandable space constraints) Not very clear background information on the quantum theory
3. Missing details on implementation required for reproducibility

In the current version of the paper I would vote for rejection, but I believe it can possibly be changed during the discussion period to be ready for publication. The main drawback that I see in this submission is that it is claimed to be based on maths but in fact the maths is quite loose (to ignore admitted by the authors limitation of the specific case for weak Guassian noise augmentation). For example, Theorem 4.1 states that S(\rho) \approx S(\tilde(\rho)), but how close this approximation is? Or, in Lemma 4.2 the inequality holds with the approximations mentioned above it but it is never specified in the lemma itself, and again it is not specified how close these approximations are. 
Therefore, I see two ways how this submission can be amended to be publishable. Either the maths should be made more precise in the paper, or it should loosen the claims that everything is based on solid maths. If either is done during the discussion period, I am willing to increase my score. That is to say that I believe the paper contains an interesting idea and even without the strong reliance on the maths it has enough material to be published. It can be reformulated as a first step inspired by the principled approach (or if possible to make the maths precise and make the paper even stronger). 

Specific comments/suggestions (not too important for the assessment unless supporting the statements above, but rather suggestions to further improve the paper):
1. Notations H(Z) and S(Z) are redundant in abstract and only overwhelms it.
2. Introduction, the first paragraph. “the need for negative samples” - this need has not been discussed yet (apart from the abstract) and therefore looks like coming out of nowhere
3. All variables should be introduced
4. Introduction. “our derivation is based on the inequality” - unclear and weird wording
5. Introduction. “and no other trick is used” - maybe too informal
6. All acronyms should be introduced, for example, MI
7. Section 2, Non-contrastive methods. A little bit more context would be appreciated, e.g. for “representation collapse”, “cluster”, “stop-gradient”
8. Definition of the superposition state in Section 3. Are there any conditions on a and b?
9. Section 3 in general may be too brief. I appreciate it is difficult to compress the whole theory in a small section of the paper, but, for example, it was not clear for me from the initial reading that the density operator is a matrix apparently.
10. Proof of Theorem 5.1. “For x_2 ‘in X_2… ” - unclear where this statement comes from
11. Algorithm 1. f and g are not introduced
12. ImageNet-10 and ImageNet-100 - what are the classes that were randomly subsampled?
13. Table 1 font is too small



Minor:
1. Abstract. “It is also commonly known as A negative sampling size problem”
2. Introduction, third paragraph. “frequently based on A non-contrastive loss”
3. Section 3. “Note that THE hypersphere constraint…”
4. Section 6. “Considering that we did NOT try”
content.summary_of_the_review:
*Update after rebuttal* I have read the authors’ responses, other reviews and updated submission. I would like to thank the authors for their substantial revision and responses. Although the authors did address my point of adjusting wording in order not claim strong reliance on maths, the loose maths is still there. Moreover, other reviews raised valid concerns. In particular, the authors agreed that theorem 5.1 does not stand. Since no revisions are allowed anymore, I am leaving my score unchanged as I cannot see those changes the authors suggested to mitigate incorrectness of theorem 5.1. 
I would like to encourage the authors address all the comments and resubmit to another venue as I liked the overall idea of the paper.

===============


To summarise the above, I liked the idea of the paper. I am not too much familiar with the related literature, but the idea appears to be novel and intriguing. It is always interesting to see how ideas are brought from different fields. And if in fact considering the different entropy other than Shannon can help with the big batch size problem for representation learning based on mutual information estimation, it would be a very valuable and important contribution to the community. However, in the current version of the paper, it is overselling the fact that it is based on principled maths when in fact the maths is not very precise. The content of the paper is interesting enough to be published without precise maths, but I believe the paper should be revised to reflect this. Therefore, I am willing to increase the score in two cases: a) the maths is made more precise, or b) the wording of the paper is adjusted to not claim the strong reliance on the maths.

replying_to: Replying to Mutual Information Estimation as a Difference of Entropies for Unsupervised Representation Learning
display_title: Official Review of Paper3965 by Reviewer heVY

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes an approach for unsupervised representation learning (with a focus on visual problems) that minimizes a loss function that can be regarded as an upper bound of the negative mutual information. 

The loss is constructed by nothing that $I(z_1; z_2) = h(z_1)-h(z_1|z_2)$, by using von Neumann's entropy as lower bound for Shannon entropy $h(z_1)$, and by noting that the conditional entropy term can be upper-bounded as $h(z_1|z_2) \leq \alpha - \beta E[\cos(z_1, z_2)]$ for some $\alpha$ and $\beta$.
content.main_review:
**Strength:** Empirical results seem promising.

**Weaknesses:** 

**I) The Main Claim is Off:** 
The paper claims to propose "a principled mutual information estimator that is not contrastive and utilizes a difference of entropies formulation". However, as a mutual information estimator, the approach proposed herein has too many shortcomings:

- The estimator is *not consistent* and is *asymptotically biased* (i.e. we can't get close enough to the true mutual information, irrespective of the amount of data available).

- The estimator only applies to vectors of the same size (otherwise we wouldn't be able to calculate the cosine similarity). However, many usecases require estimating the mutual information between vectors of different sizes (e.g. [2]).

- The proposed algorithm has many flaws (see below).

**II) Technical Issues:** 
- **$\beta$ should not be a hyper-parameter (if the authors want the loss function used to estimate the negative mutual information)**. Theorem 5.1. provides that for two random variables $z_1=f(x_1)$ and $z_2=f(x_2)$ ***there exist*** $\alpha$ and $\beta$ for which $h(z_1|z_2) \leq \alpha - \beta E[\cos(z_1, z_2)]$. To obtain a lower-bound on the mutual information, $\alpha - \beta E[\cos(z_1, z_2)]$ *does* need to be an upper-bound of $h(z_1|z_2)$. Not only can the authors not choose any $\beta$, but the right $\beta$ actually depends on $f$ (i.e. technically speaking, it is a function of parameters of the encoding and projection networks).

-  ****$\alpha$** has been unduly omitted from Algorithm 1**. On the face of it, it does not seem as though $\alpha$ depends on any parameter, and as such one would think it can be conveniently omitted from the loss function. However, the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ as per Theorem 5.1. *do* depend on $f$ (i.e. on the parameters of the encoding and projection networks). 

If the authors want the loss function to be an upper bound of the negative mutual information, both $\alpha$ and $\beta$ should be included in the loss function, and their dependencies on parameters of $f$ should be explicitly taken into account in gradient calculation.


**III) Incomplete Litterature Review:**

[1] Showed that most of the fundamental limitations described by [3], in particular the $O(\log n)$ upper bound and the high estimation variance, can be alleviated when working in the copula-uniform dual space (i.e. the image of the input space by the probability integral transform of each coordinate). Additionally, [2] (Appendix A) proved that, when applied in the copula-uniform dual space, the DV characterization of the KL divergence can be viewed as a mini-max copula entropy problem, and the resulting estimator does not suffer from the formal limitations in [3].


[1] Samo, Y.L.K., 2021, March. Inductive Mutual Information Estimation: A Convex Maximum-Entropy Copula Approach. In International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (pp. 2242-2250). PMLR.

[2] Samo, Y.L.K., 2021. LeanML: A Design Pattern To Slash Avoidable Wastes in Machine Learning Projects. arXiv preprint arXiv:2107.08066.

[3] McAllester, D. and Stratos, K., 2020, June. Formal limitations on the measurement of mutual information. In International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (pp. 875-884). PMLR.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The approach proposed herein can hardly be regarded as a mutual information estimator. 

Despite the interesting link to quantum information theory, and the effort to relate the loss function used in Algorithm 1 to an upper bound of the negative mutual information obtained as a difference of entropies, at the end of the day, the authors simply use as similarity metrics the function $\mathcal{S}(z_1, z_2) := S(z_1)+\beta E[\cos(z_1, z_2)]$, not the mutual information $I(z_1; z_2)$.

It is not surprising that $-\mathcal{S}$ works well in practice as a loss function to find good feature representations:

- The von Neumann entropy term $S(z_1)$ effectively mitigates redundant features and high variance features. Indeed, it promotes uniformity among eigenvalues of $\tilde{\rho}$. Noting that $\tilde{\rho}$ can be viewed as a sample autocovariance matrix of $z_1$, $S(z_1)$ implicitly pushes the eigenbasis of $\tilde{\rho}$ towards the canonical basis of $\mathbb{R}^d$, and in so doing it also pushes features to be decorrelated and have the same variance $1/d$ (given that $\tilde{\rho}$ has trace $1$).

- The cosine similarity term $E[\cos(z_1, z_2)]$ on the other hand ensures that the learned representation is only mildly affected by small input perturbations.

I would have had a more favorable opinion of the paper, had the authors not claimed to introduce a new mutual information estimator, and had they focused instead on unsupervised representation learning as an application.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Authors' response
content.comment:
Thank you very much for your review. We fully agree with you on your feedback of “the main claim is off”, and we did our best to clean up the clumsy writings. Regarding this, we would appreciate it if you could check the “General response to all reviewers” on top of this page. In our defense, we never intended to say we are proposing a new mutual information estimation method, but clearly some of the sentences were clumsy and misleading. We are sorry for our mistakes.The below are specific responses to your comments.

R2-#1 The main claim is off: Right. Besides the extensive revisions, we also changed the title. 

R2-#2 Technical issues: We agree, and we hope these issues are resolved because our contribution is a new loss function and not a mutual information estimator.   

R2-#3: Incomplete literature review: Thanks for letting us know of the works. We were not aware of [1] and [2], and indeed [1] is quite relevant. We have updated the related work section, and have mentioned that it might be possible to develop a new unsupervised learning method based on the work in [1]. Please see the first paragraph on page 4. 

R2-#4 Regarding your comment “The von Neumann entropy term $S(z_1)$ effectively mitigates redundant features and high variance features...”: 
Thanks for the comment. We believe there are two types of approaches on developing a new unsupervised learning technique. The first type is to start from mutual information, develop bounds or approximations, and design a corresponding loss. The second type is to start from a high level concept(s) such as uniformity/alignment, redundancy-reduction principle (Barlow-twins), etc., and to develop a corresponding loss. While our work falls into the first type, we certainly believe a similar loss could have been designed by starting from an adequate high-level concept. Nonetheless, we believe the first type is preferred because of the knowledge and insights we can gain from the related theories. In fact, this is the main contribution of our work - a high-performance non-contrastive loss for unsupervised learning that can be related to the elegant theories of quantum information theory.

replying_to: Replying to Authors' response

content.title: Thanks for your response
content.comment:
Thanks for your response. I've read it and the revised paper with attention. 

While I have a slightly more positive view of the work in its totality after you removed references to mutual information estimation, I still think your message does not line up with the proposed algorithm (Algorithm 1).

**I- Contrary to your claims, Algorithm 1 does not minimize the conditional entropy.**
- **Your proof of Theorem 5.1. is incorrect:** In your proof you attempt to show that if $e := x_2-x_1$ is Gaussian (with a small variance) and $f$ is piecewise-linear, then $e_f := f(x_2)-f(x_1)$ ought to be Gaussian. This is incorrect. Saying that $f$ is piecewise-linear is equivalent to saying that $f(x) = \sum_i (A_ix +b_i) \mathbb{1}(x \in \mathcal{B}_i)$ for some partition $(\mathcal{B}_i)_i$ of the input domain. Thus, $f(x_1) = \sum_i (A_ix_1 +b_i) \mathbb{1}(x_1 \in \mathcal{B}_i)$ and $f(x_2) = \sum_i (A_i(x_1+e) +b_i) \mathbb{1}(x_1+e \in \mathcal{B}_i)$. Note that, even when $e$ has a very small variance, conditional on $x_1$, the indicator terms $\mathbb{1}(x_1+e \in \mathcal{B}_i)$ are random; they are Bernouilli distributed! Hence, $f(x_2)$ isn't necessarily Gaussian conditional on $x_1$, which implies, $e_f:=f(x_2)-f(x_1)$ isn't necessarily Gaussian. The mistake you made is to think that because $e$ has a small variance, if $x_1 \in \mathcal{B}_i$ then $x_1+e \in \mathcal{B}_i$. This is not true. No matter how small the variance of $e$, its support is $\mathbb{R}$, and there is a non-null probability that $x_1+e \notin \mathcal{B}_i$ despite $x_1 \in \mathcal{B}_i$. This non-null probability, no matter how small, is sufficient to cause $e_f$ not to be Gaussian. Hence, you cannot apply your Theorem 4.4. to conclude. Here's a more qualitative illustration that your proof of Theorem 5.1 is incorrect. You want to prove that $h(z_1|z_2) \leq \alpha - \beta E(\cos (z_1, z_2))$, for some $\alpha$ and $\beta$. The left hand side is a ***distribution (or global) property***, specifically a property of the joint distribution of $(x_1, x_2)$ and the feature transformation $f$. However, in the proof you establish that $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are related to the eigenvalues of the matrix $cAA^T$, where $A$ comes from the local linear representation of $f$ in the neighborhood of a specific value of $x_1$. In other words, the right hand side of the inequality you claim to have proved is a  ***sample (or local) property***. This doesn't make sense.

- **Even if Theorem 5.1. was correct, both** $\alpha$ **and** $\beta$ **should be included in Algorithm 1 as functions of the feature transformation, not as hyper-parameters, if you want Algorithm 1 to minimize the conditional entropy** $h(z_1|z_2)$. In your own proof of Theorem 5.1., for $\alpha - \beta E(\cos (z_1, z_2))$ to be an upper-bound of the conditional entropy $h(z_1|z_2)$, both $\alpha$ and $\beta$ need to depend on $f$ (through eigenvalues of the matrix $cAA^T$). However, in Algorithm 1 you omit $\alpha$ and consider $\beta$ a hyper-parameter. Hence, Algorithm 1 does not support the narrative that you are minimizing an upper bound of the conditional entropy $h(z_1|z_2)$. Assuming Theorem 5.1. was correct, to do this, you would need to include the dependencies of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ on parameters of $f$ in the calculation of the gradient of your loss function. 

**II- It is unclear to me why you would want to minimize the conditional entropy in this application.**

Now that you've agreed to focus on a loss function for representation learning, it is unclear to me why you would want to minimize the conditional entropy $h(z_1|z_2)$ in this context. I appreciate you wanting to ground your work in information theory (and quantum mechanics), but if the first term is an entropy term (von Neumann in your case), the second term ought to be the only term that will ensure that the feature transformation produces the **same** result despite the chosen data augmentation procedure (in this case an additive Gaussian permutation). You cannot get this property using the conditional entropy $h(z_1|z_2)$ as conditional entropies have a few invariances (e.g. for any smooth invertible transformation $t$, $h(z_1| t(z_2)) = h(z_1|z_2)$). While these invariance properties are a 'feature' in many applications, they seem to be a 'bug' to me in this application. As an alternative, the cosine similarity term is only scale-invariant, which isn't a problem per se as your feature transformation is normalized. 

Overall, it seems a bit odd to me that you'd want to frame the cosine similarity as an approximation/proxy for the conditional entropy, even though the cosine similarity would provide a stronger sense of robustness to data augmentation than the conditional entropy.


**III- Re: Your #4***

My aim was to provide an intuitive reason why I expect Algorithm 1 to work well in practice for representation learning, despite it not being aligned with the core message as discussed above.

content.title: Authors' response
content.comment:
R2-2ndRound-#1: Contrary to your claims, Algorithm 1 does not minimize the conditional entropy.

While it might be possible to address the first issue ($e_f$ not being Gaussian), the second issue ($\alpha$ and $\beta$ being dependent on $f$) indeed makes the theorem incorrect. Therefore, we agree that Theorem 5.1 does not stand. Thank you very much for pointing out the flaw.  

The issue was also pointed out by reviewer 1 (7tZk; comment #7). 

Because Section 5 deals with the loss design, the following seems to be the best direction for a revision. 

1. Rather than considering an assumption at input level (X), we can directly adopt an assumption at the representation level (Z). 
2. Empirically, $\mathbf{Z}_1\sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{Z}_2,\Sigma)$ can be shown. We have confirmed this for our unsupervised learning experiments. To be precise, the covariance of $z_d = z_2-z_1$ converges to a diagonal matrix (that is not far from a scaled identity matrix) and each neuron’s distribution also follows a Gaussian distribution. The Gaussian distribution is expected and confirmed for randomly initialized weights, and its peak becomes slightly larger once the training is complete. 
3. The empirical results in #2 is not limited to a particular augmentation. We verified #2 for SimCLR’s augmentation that is drastically different from the weak Gaussian augmentation.    
4. It has been known that representation can be shown to follow Gaussian distributions in some cases. (references will be provided)
5. Based on #2, #3, and #4, we will revise Section 5 as below. 

   a. Remove Theorem 5.1 that is incorrect

   b. Explain why $\mathbf{Z}_1\sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{Z}_2,\Sigma)$ can be a reasonable assumption. Provide empirical results in appendix.

   c. Explain how cosine similarity term in the loss design can be motivated by Theorem 4.4 and the empirical observations. 


The above revision has a downside of depending on the empirical distribution assumption, but an upside is that the limitation on weak Gaussian augmentation can be removed. Any augmentation design that empirically results in $\mathbf{Z}_1\sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{Z}_2,\Sigma)$ can be motivated. 

For a practical implementation, the planned revision might be more relevant because the result is not limited to the weak Gaussian augmentation any more. However, we fully recognize that the scope of the contribution will change (despite a limited revision that we expect)...

replying_to: Replying to Authors' response

content.title: Re: Authors' response
content.comment:
**I- You might want to take the results of your experiments about** $z_d$ **with a pinch of salt.**

For any function $f$ that is smooth (at least $C^1$) in the neighborhood of $x_1$, we have $e_f := f(x_1 +e) - f(x_1) =  Df(x_1)e + o(||e||)$, where $Df(x)$ is the Jacobian matrix of $f$ at $x$ (first order Taylor's expansion).

Note that when $e \sim \mathcal{N}(0, c)$ with a small $c$, the residual term $o(||e||)$ will be very small with high probability, so that, in practice, you will have a hard time telling samples from $e_f$ apart from samples from $\bar{e}_f := Df(x_1)e$. 

Noting that $\bar{e}_f \sim \mathcal{N}\left(0, cE(Df(x_1)Df(x_1)^T) \right)$, you can see why your experiments might point to the fact that $e_f$ is Gaussian (conditional on $x_1$) when in fact it is not. Its tails, which you will hardly observe in your experiments, will be different from tails of $\bar{e}_f$.

Additionally, when $f$ is piecewise linear, the error term vanishes much quicker! In fact,  $e_f =  Df(x_1)e + o(||e||^q)$ for any $q > 1$, so long as $f$ is $q$ times differentiable in a neighborhood of $x$. 

While $e_f \neq Df(x_1)e$, in practice you will need a high enough value of $e$ to see the difference. Specifically, and referring to my previous comment, you need a value of $e$ so that $x_1 \in \mathcal{B}_i$ but $x_1+e \in \mathcal{B}_j$, with $j\neq i$. By choosing a small error variance $c$, you are only making it less likely for you to see this happen in your experiments; you are not making $e_f$ Gaussian.

Speaking of $c$, you probably want to make any assumption on $c$ more rigorous than $c \to 0$. $c$ is a set value, not a limit. More importantly, $c$ reflects the level of noise to which the feature map will be resilient.

As for why in your experiments the covariance matrix of $e_f$ ($ \approx cE(Df(x_1)Df(x_1)^T)$) might appear near-diagonal, this likely has to do with the von Neumann entropy term shrinking coordinates of $f(x)$ towards decorrelation. See my first review.

**II- Even assuming Gaussianity, Theorem 4.4. still does not apply.**

In the most general form of a conditional distribution $P_{z_2 | z_1}$, the distribution parameters ***depend*** on $z_1$! However, in Section 4.2 (Lemma 4.3 and subsequently Theorem 4.4), you implicitly made the ***very strong*** assumption that, conditional on $z_1$, $z_2$ is Gaussian with mean $0$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma$ that ***does not depend on*** $z_1$!

So, even if one ignores my **I-** above and concedes to you the argument that $z_2$ is Gaussian conditional on $z_1$, its conditional covariance matrix would be that of $e_f$, namely $cE(Df(x_1)Df(x_1)^T)$, which clearly does depend on $x_1$! Thus, if you cannot apply Theorem 4.4 at the feature level. 

When $\Sigma$ depends on $Z_2$, in your proof of Theorem 4.4 you cannot take eigenvalues out of integrals as constants.

**III- Better notations could help easily detect/avoid those mathematical flaws**

You might want to adopt more rigorous notations. Instead of $Z_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(Z_2, \Sigma)$, you should have written $Z_1| Z_2 \sim \mathcal{N}(Z_2, \Sigma)$. Had you done this, you might not have made the mistake I raised in **II-**.

content.title: Authors' response
content.comment:
* R2-2ndRound-#2: It is unclear to me why you would want to minimize the conditional entropy in this …

We have a slightly different opinion on this. As you have pointed out, a single message does not necessarily need to be encoded into a single codeword. Furthermore, it is unclear if one-to-one mapping is really a better encoding scheme for unsupervised learning, even under the limitation of linear evaluation (i.e. a linear decoder). Let us elaborate using two of the popular unsupervised learning methods as examples. 

For BYOL and SimSiam, a predictor $h(\cdot)$ is required for learning (for the diagram in Figure 1, $h(\cdot)$ is additionally inserted right after $Z_1$). This means the learning does not care about having a single unique representation for each input image, and only aims to have $h(z_1)=z_2$. The implication of this equation can be different between BYOL and SimSiam. For SimSiam, a common (stochastic) augmentation function is used for both paths. Therefore, the learning aims for $h(z_2)=z_1$ as well as $h(z_1)=z_2$ by symmetry. In fact, $z_1$ can be replaced with the representation of any other instance of augmentation. When all possible augmentations are considered together, the set of all equality constraints together is quite restrictive. For BYOL, two different augmentation functions are used for the two paths and the learning does not aim for $h(z_2)=z_1$ while pursuing $h(z_1)=z_2$. Still, $h(z_1) \doteq z_1'=z_2$ needs to be satisfied for all possible combinations of augmentations and the learning aims for a single unique representation $z_1'=z_2$ for each input image. However, $z_1$ does not need to be unique if $h(\cdot)$ is not invertible. The input null space of $h(\cdot)$ allows $z_1$ to vary depending on the choice of augmentation in the upper path. It is not clear if this relaxed inductive bias is helpful for representation learning, but it is certainly an interesting one. It is also possible to add such a flexibility to the lower path by adding $h_2(\cdot)$ to the lower path. On a separate but related topic, the use of momentum encoder in BYOL's lower path does not affect the above discussion. It forces the two encoders to be related but different and thus $z_1\neq z_2$ is possible even for $x_1=x_2$. This effect of having two different representation spaces can be certainly allowed for BYOL, but probably not desirable for SimCLR that aim for a unique representation. The implication to SimSiam is unclear. 

The outstanding performance of BYOL and SimSiam indicates that forcing a unique representation through cosine similarity might not be the best solution. In general, there seems to be many open problems related to unsupervised learning and uniqueness of the representation is one of them. In any case, it looks like the research stream based on MI has been extremely helpful for the heuristics based pretext learning methods to evolve into the current contrastive and non-contrastive learning methods.

replying_to: Replying to Authors' response

content.title: Re: Authors' response
content.comment:
**Re: the scope of my comment.**

My comment was specific to a setup described by Figure 1 (where the same functions $f$ and $g$ are applied to both branches). As I said in a previous comment, I can easily see why the invariances of conditional entropies could be a 'feature' in other schemes; I am just not sure that is the case when the same functions are applied to both branches (as in Figure 1). To be clear, this does not motivate my overall appreciation of the paper: the following related points do.

**Re: The outstanding performance of BYOL and SimSiam indicates that forcing a unique representation through cosine similarity might not be the best solution.**

That's a problem! Algorithm 1 maximizes the cosine similarity, it does not the minimize conditional entropy. So if you are set on the idea that maximizing the cosine similarity isn't so great, then you should rewrite Algorithm 1. 

Critically, you **cannot** upper-bound $h(z_2|z_1)$ with $\alpha - \beta E(\cos (z_1, z_2))$, ***even in the case of Gaussian augmentation***, as I formally prove below.

***Proposition A:*** One cannot find $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{R}$ such that for ***all*** random variables $z_1$ and $z_2$ such that $z_2-z_1$ is a centrered Gaussian, $h(z_2|z_1) \leq \alpha - \beta E(\cos(z_2, z_1))$.

***Implications of A:*** In other words, you cannot find a one-size-fits-all set of hyper-parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$ such that $h(z_2|z_1) \leq \alpha - \beta E(\cos(z_1, z_2))$ whenever $z_2-z_1$ is Gaussian. If the inequality holds in the case of Gaussian augmentation, then $\alpha$ and/or $\beta$ **ought to depend on the covariance matrix** of $z_2-z_1$, which you would not know at the beginning of Algorithm 1, and which would vary throughout the runtime of the algorithm as a function of network parameters. 

***Proof of Proposition A:*** Let's assume Proposition A is false and we can find such $\alpha$ and $\beta$. Then we have $h(z_2|z_1) \leq |\alpha| + |\beta|$ for any distributions $z_1$ and $z_2$, so long as $z_2-z_1$ is Gaussian. Clearly that's absurd. Indeed if $z_2 - z_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma)$, then $h(z_2|z_1) = \frac{1}{2} \log ((2\pi e)^d \det \Sigma)$, which cannot be upper-bounded for all $\Sigma$. This is because $\det \Sigma \leq \prod_{i=1}^d \Sigma_{ii}$, so that you may always choose a diagonal (conditional variance) term that makes the conditional entropy larger than $|\alpha| + |\beta|$.

Even if you impose an upperbound condition on the determinant of the covariance matrix of $z_2-z_1$, hoping that you could then find $\alpha$ and $\beta$ such that $h(z_2|z_1) \leq \alpha - \beta E(\cos(z_1, z_2))$ so long as $z_2-z_1$ is centered and Gaussian with covariance matrix $\Sigma$ satisfying $\det \Sigma \leq \xi$, there would still be a problem.

Not only will you still have to prove that such $\alpha$ and $\beta$ exist (the determinant condition kills my proof of non-existence, it does not prove existence), but **even if they do exist**, for all practical purposes, **minimizing your upper-bound would not amount to minimizing the conditional entropy.**

Indeed, $\alpha - \beta E(\cos(z_1, z_2)) \geq \alpha-|\beta|$. Yet, $h(z_2|z_1)$ can be made arbitrarily small (down to $-\inf$) by simply making any diagonal term $\Sigma_{ii}$ arbitrarily small (which would not violate the low-determinant condition). The gap $|h(z_2|z_1)-\alpha+|\beta||$ can be so big that basically maximizing $E(\cos(z_1, z_2))$ will have no effect on $h(z_2|z_1)$, especially when the Gaussian augmentation is 'weak'.

content.title: Authors' response
content.comment:
Thanks for the careful review and feedback. It is quite inspiring and helpful to hear your thoughts, and we truly appreciate your time and thoughts. Now, here are some of our thoughts. 

We do not believe maximizing cosine similarity is either great or not great. In fact, we do not believe MI formulation is either great or not great for the unsupervised learning performance, either. With our best knowledge, none of the existing works was able to conclude one way or the other (most of the works focused on empirically improving the benchmark performance).  Apparently, our work cannot answer the questions, either. All we are claiming in this work is that there is a non-contrastive learning algorithm that can be designed with von Neumann entropy and cosine similarity, where the design starts from a DoE formulation of MI. The resulting algorithm achieves an outstanding performance, which makes our non-Contrastive algorithm interesting and relevant. Since we were not able to come up with a quantum loss for the conditional entropy part, at least we tried to show how cosine similarity can be motivated from a bound. While we are not sure of the exact role of MI, we still believe MI is much more likely to help us understand how unsupervised learning works (when compared to the existing non-contrastive algorithms) and therefore we tried our best to stay within an information theoretic framework. 

In our result, we are assuming a fixed covariance matrix $\Sigma$ for the entire training process. We agree that this assumption can be too strong because $\Sigma$ will certainly vary as the training proceeds. To address this issue, perhaps we can come up with additional empirical results and additional assumptions on how much $\Sigma$ can vary during the training, but that’s beyond what we wanted to show. All we are showing is that cosine similarity loss becomes relevant when $z_d$ follows a Gaussian distribution with a fixed $\Sigma$. We understand that this result is quite limited, but it is certainly a better one than empirically showing that cosine similarity performs better than cross-entropy for a few benchmark cases. Also, a more rigorous result will likely cause a significant complication in the interpretation and derivation, and we didn’t want that. Rather, our contribution lies in Algorithm 1 that is non-contrastive, simple, works well for small batch-size and small number of epochs (this is important unless one has an access to heavy computing resources like V100/A100; we don’t...), based on von Neumann entropy, and works well for the popular benchmarks.  

Architecture design (e.g. inclusion of a predictor  $h(\cdot)$) is a main tool for the researchers to control certain aspects of learning, but there is no guarantee that we will see the intended results due to the SGD being the main workhorse of the learning - we cannot fully control the learning dynamics anyway. While we provided examples of SimSiam and BYOL where  $h(\cdot)$ is used, there is no reason to assume that SimCLR architecture cannot learn similar representations as BYOL and SimSiam as long as proper loss functions are used. The choice of cosine similarity with SimCLR will likely force SGD to learn a single codeword for an input, but the choice does not need to be limited to cosine similarity even when SimCLR architecture is used. Therefore, we didn’t really set a target on what to show. Instead, we investigated many possibilities and we are reporting what we were able to find, because we think they will be useful for moving forward.

content.title: Revised Summary Review
content.comment:
Thanks for the kind words.

I think the fundamental mistake you've been making throughout is to try to equate your loss terms (von Neumann entropy and cosine similarity) to mutual information components (entropy and conditional entropy) or bounds thereof, which you really don't need in order to ground Algorithm 1 in information theory.

It is crucial for you to realize that, if Algorithm 1 works, it is ***not*** because you are implicitly estimating features' entropy and conditional entropy, or maximizing/minimizing bounds thereof. 

As I mentioned and proved in my comment above, with $\alpha$ omitted and $\beta$ considered a hyper-parameter, the cosine similarity term ***cannot*** be regarded as an upper bound of the conditional entropy, even if you assume features are Gaussian. More importantly, with $\alpha$ omitted and $\beta$ considered a hyper-parameter, maximizing the cosine similarity term ***cannot*** be regarded as minimizing the conditional entropy!

Note in passing that, if you assume that features $(z_1, z_2)$ are jointly Gaussian, then the conditional entropy $h(z_1|z_2)$ is available in closed-form and reads: $h(z_1|z_2) = \frac{d}{2} \log(2\pi e) + \frac{1}{2} \left( \log \det \Sigma_{12, 12} - \log \det \Sigma_{2,2}\right)$, where $\Sigma_{12,12}$ is the autocovariance matrix of $(z_1, z_2)$ and $\Sigma_{2,2}$ is the autocovariance matrix $z_2$. 

In other words, under the Gaussian assumption for features, you don't need the cosine similarity if your goal is to minimize the conditional entropy!

Taking a step back, if you want to stick to Algorithm 1 as-is, and provide a theoretical justification for it, rather than trying to prove that your loss terms *are bounds* of mutual information terms (which they are not), you could focus instead on conveying that **they play the same roles** as mutual information terms, as far self-supervised learning goes.

I'll elaborate on this in subsequent comments; hopefully, they help you in subsequent revisions.

replying_to: Replying to Revised Summary Review

content.title: Re: Revised Summary Review
content.comment:
In my opinion, the two tenets of self-supervised learning are i) the feature map should be ***rich***, and ii) the feature map should be ***robust to desired data augmentations***.

**Richness:** Given a code size, the feature map should pack as much information as possible in the feature vector. In particular, features should not be redundant, and the feature map should not degenerate into producing the same codeword.

**Robustness to data augmentation:** The feature vectors $z_1$ and $z_2$ resulting from two augmented input vectors should be, if not identical, very similar statistically.

**I- The Case of Mutual Information**

Let us consider the identity $I(z_1; z_2) = h(z_1) - h(z_1|z_2)$. 

The *richness* tenet is satisfied by maximizing the entropy term $h(z_1)$. 

Indeed, noting that $h(z_1) = h(u_{z_1}) + \sum_{i=1}^d h(z_1[i])$, where $h(u_{z_1})$ is the entropy of the copula of coordinates of $z_1$, you can see that maximizing $h(z_1)$ is equivalent to maximizing the entropy of individual features (which guards against single-codeword collapse) and maximizing the entropy of the copula (which guards against dependent features/inefficient codes).

The *robustness to data augmentation* tenet is satisfied by minimizing the conditional entropy term $h(z_1|z_2)$. 

Indeed, given $z_1$, minimizing $h(z_1|z_2)$ is equivalent to maximizing how informative $z_2$ is about $z_1$, or how statistically similar both are.

Overall, maximizing mutual information could work well for self-supervised learning [...] if it wasn't for the fact that mutual information estimation is quite hard, as you rightly pointed out in the paper.

replying_to: Replying to Re: Revised Summary Review

content.title: Re: Revised Summary Review
content.comment:
**II- Beyond Mutual Information**

As previously mentioned, mutual information estimation is hard. So are estimating $h(z_1)$ (resp. $h(z_1|z_2)$), and maximizing a lower bound of $h(z_1)$ (resp. minimizing an upper bound of $h(z_1|z_2)$) without making distribution assumptions.

To me, as far as self-supervised learning goes, $h(z_1)$ and $h(z_1|z_2)$ are only useful to the extent that they satisfy the two tenets mentioned above; it is unclear to me what value maximizing/minimizing them would add beyond said tenets.

So, if you could find inspiration in $h(z_1)$ and $h(z_1|z_2)$ to construct loss terms that satisfy the two tenets **and** are tractable. Here are some ideas consistent with Algorithm 1.

**i) Richness** 

You can find inspiration in $h(z_1)$ to construct an easy-to-evaluate information-theoretic richness term. 

A trick to make things tractable is to focus on the second-order in your thinking of richness, and discard higher moments as an approximation. 

Let $\Sigma_{1,1}$ be the autocorrelation matrix of $z_1$, and $0 \leq \lambda_1 \leq \dots \leq \lambda_d$ its eigenvalues. 

The 'richest' (or most efficient) feature map is the one whose correlation matrix is the identity matrix, and it has eigenvalues $\lambda_i = d$ and corresponding eigenbasis the canonical basis of $\mathbb{R}^d$. 

The single codeword degenerate scenario (the least efficient feature map) corresponds to $\Sigma_{1,1}$ having all entries set to 1, and the associated eigenvalues are $\lambda_d=d$, $\lambda_i=0$ for $i<d$.

By the conservation of the trace, $ \sum_{i=1}^d \Sigma_{1,1}[i,i] = d = \sum_{i=1}^d \lambda_i$. Thus $\Omega := (\omega_1, \dots, \omega_d)$ with $\omega_i = \frac{\lambda_i}{d}$ defines a discrete probability distribution. 

$M := (\frac{1}{d}, \dots, \frac{1}{d})$ is the probability distribution corresponding to the best-case scenario (the 'richest' feature map). It also happens to be the maximum entropy distribution out of all discrete distributions with $d$ outcomes. 

$m := (1, 0, \dots, 0)$ is the probability distribution corresponding to the worst-case (single codeword degenerate) scenario. It also happens to be the minimum entropy distribution out of all discrete distributions with $d$ outcomes. 

**Using** $-\sum_{i=1}^d \lambda_i \log \lambda_i$ **as richness term:**
- **Discrete Entropy Narrative:** A natural richness term is therefore the Shannon entropy of the distribution induced by eigenvalues: $H(\Omega) := -\sum_{i=1}^d \omega_i \log \omega_i = \log d -\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i=1}^d \lambda_i \log \lambda_i$. Note that maximizing $H(\Omega)$ is the same as maximizing your von Neumann entropy term $S(z_1) :=-\sum_{i=1}^d \lambda_i \log \lambda_i$.

- **KL Divergence Narrative:** It is also worth noting that $KL(\Omega || M) = \sum_{i=1}^d \omega_i \log(d\omega_i) = \log d - H(\Omega) = \frac{1}{d}\sum_{i=1}^d \lambda_i \log \lambda_i$. Thus, maximizing $H(\Omega)$, maximizing $S(z_1)$ and minimizing $KL(\Omega || M)$ are basically the same thing.

**Using** $-\sum_{i=1}^d \log \lambda_i$ **as richness term:**

- **Reverse KL Divergence Narrative:** The KL divergence perspective above is useful because you could also have minimized the KL divergence in the opposite direction: $KL(M || \Omega) = \sum_{i=1}^d \frac{1}{d} \log(d\omega_i) = -\frac{1}{d} \sum_{i=1}^d \log \lambda_i = -\frac{1}{d} \log \det \Sigma_{1,1}$. Minimizing $KL(M || \Omega)$ is therefore equivalent to maximizing the log-determinant of the correlation matrix of features, which makes intuitive sense as an approach for maximizing richness.

- **Maximum-Entropy Narrative:** Here's another insight. We could also have arrived at maximizing $\log \det \Sigma_{1,1}$ using a maximum entropy argument. Once we have decided to ensure richness solely through $\Sigma_{1,1}$, instead of maximizing $h(z_1)$ (using the real distribution of $z_1$, which we do not know), we could maximize the entropy of the maximum-entropy distribution, out of all candidate distributions whose *autocovariance* matrices are $\Sigma_{1,1}$, the autocorrelation matrix of $z_1$. Said maximum-entropy distribution is a Gaussian with covariance matrix $\Sigma_{1,1}$ and its entropy is 
$\frac{d}{2} \log(2\pi e) + \frac{1}{2} \log \det \Sigma_{1,1}$.

While considering $-\sum_{i=1}^d \log \lambda_i$ gave us some interesting theoretical insights, $-\sum_{i=1}^d \lambda_i \log \lambda_i$ should be preferred for two reasons. 

First, $-\sum_{i=1}^d \lambda_i \log \lambda_i$  is always well-defined (using the convention $0\log 0 = 0$) unlike $-\sum_{i=1}^d \log \lambda_i$ which breaks down when any eigenvalue is $0$ (i.e. at least one feature is a linear combination of the others).

Second, $-\sum_{i=1}^d \lambda_i \log \lambda_i \in [0, \log d]$ whereas $-\sum_{i=1}^d \log \lambda_i$ is unbounded. The unboundedness of $-\sum_{i=1}^d \log \lambda_i$ can be problematic when it is paired with a bounded data augmentation robustness loss term (e.g. the cosine similarity).

replying_to: Replying to Re: Revised Summary Review

content.title: Re: Revised Summary Review
content.comment:
**ii) Robustness to data augmentation**

Here we simply need to use a term that expresses that $z_1$ and $z_2$ are 'close enough' statistically, a term that is easy to evaluate. 

There is a wide range of ideas. Here are a few:
- **Geometrically inspired**:  $E(\cos(z_1, z_2)):= E\left(\frac{z_1^Tz_2}{||z_1|| ||z_2||} \right)$
- **Mean-square error inspired**: $E(||z_1-z_2||^2)$, $\frac{E(||z_1-z_2||^2)}{\sqrt{E(||z_1||^2)E(||z_2||^2)}}$, $E\left( || \frac{z_1}{||z_1||} - \frac{z_2}{||z_2||} ||^2\right)$
- **Gaussian inspired**: $\log \det \Sigma_{12, 12} - \log \det \Sigma_{2, 2}$ (conditional entropy $h(z_1|z_2)$ when $(z_1, z_2)$ is Gaussian), $\text{Tr}\left(\Sigma_{1,2} \Sigma_{2,2}^{-1} \Sigma_{1,2}^T \right)$ (the sum of the reductions of variance of coordinates of $z_1$ that are observed when $z_2$ is known in the case where $(z_1, z_2)$ is Gaussian).
- **Gaussian inspired (robustified)**: We saw that $KL(M||\Omega) = -\frac{1}{d} \log \det \Sigma_{1,1}$, and $KL(\Omega || M) = \frac{1}{d} \sum_{i=1}^d \lambda_i \log \lambda_i := -\frac{1}{d} S(\Sigma_{1,1})$. Because $KL(M||\Omega)$ and $KL(\Omega||M)$ play the same role, we can use $S(\Sigma)$ as a more robust plug-in replacement for $\log \det \Sigma$. The loss term $\left( \log \det \Sigma_{12, 12} - \log \det \Sigma_{2, 2}\right)$ then becomes $S(\Sigma_{12,12})-S(\Sigma_{2,2})$.

Using the last choice of data augmentation robustness term, your final self-supervised learning objective function to maximize would take the form $O(z_1, z_2; \alpha, \beta) := \alpha S(\Sigma_{1,1}) + \beta S(\Sigma_{2,2}) - \beta S(\Sigma_{12,12})$ for hyper-parameters $\alpha, \beta > 0$. 

Note that, when $\alpha=\beta=1$, this is a mutual-information-like objective function obtained by systematically replacing differential entropies with von Neumann entropies. To be specific, $O(z_1, z_2; 1, 1)$ is the von Neumann or quantum mutual information. I'm sure you can generate a lot more insights from this observation.

**Conclusion:** I'll keep my score unchanged as the last version of the paper contains wrong results, and the main claims are still off and inconsistent with Algorithm 1. While the detailed suggestions I provided above suffice to fix the narrative and possibly extend Algorithm 1, these are substantial changes that definitely require another round of reviews.

display_title: Official Review of Paper3965 by Reviewer 7tZk

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a new approach for unsupervised representation learning through paired augmentations and mutual information maximization. A lower bound on Shannon mutual information between the random variables corresponding to the representations for two augmented instances is maximized. The surrogate is based on a form of von Neumann information from quantum information theory, along with a lower bound based on an assumption of small Gaussian perturbation between the variables in the representation space. The approach is applied to benchmarked image data sets and compares favorably for small data sets with existing unsupervised representation learning.
content.main_review:
Strengths:

The idea of using an information theoretic principled approach to unsupervised learning representation with data augmentation makes sense.

The perturbation analysis approach with von Neumann conditional entropy appears to be novel and provides a somewhat meaningful lower bound.

The experimental results are promising. The methods try to adopt approaches previously choices of augmentation. 


Weaknesses:

There is some issues with clarity and organization.

1) Reading the introduction, at the point on page 2, "we adopt cosine similarity" it is not at all clear to me as a reader how a similarity measure would be useful for gauging the conditional entropy.  Furthermore, the phrase "cosine similarity is equivalent to the loss term" isn't clear either. These statements need more explanation for a reader who hasn't seen the main results.

2) The paper does not clarify the main restriction assumption to apply von Neumann entropy to sets of vectors. It should be noted on page 2 that Shannon entropy can be directly applied to the eigenvalues since the uncentered second moment for points on the hyper-sphere yields a trace-1 matrix, where the trace is the sum of the eigenvalues.  Also the definition of the entropy alone does not clarify to the reader how the conditional entropy will be calculated even though more relationships between it and cosine similarity are discussed. 

3) It is not clear to me that the physical nature of entanglement directly relates to the concept of disentanglement in representation learning. This sounds like a profound discussion but is not elaborated on.  In the beginning of Section 3 the domain of $a$ and $b$ should be clarified as the complex field in general and that the sum of their magnitudes is 1.  Nonetheless, much of the prelude of Section 3 and 3.1 could be better condensed and readers could be referred to Nielsen & Chuang's book for the background that is not essential to the paper. Instead the paragraph could relate the description of states to the feature space of learning representations, especially with the claims of entanglement. 

4) The notation in 4.1 is not clear. $\mathbf{Z}$ is a random vector but then $\mathbf{z}^i$ is said to be a member of $\mathbf{Z}$. The definition of the second moment does not appear to be correct in the population case, unless it is a discrete measure of over a countable number of points as indicated by the sum and indexing. Rather it should be clarified that there are a sample of $n$ i.i.d. random variables coming from the discrete distribution described by $\mathbf{Z}$ now a set, and probability mass function $p(i)$. 

5) In section 5.1, a formal statement of the approximation of cosine similarity to inner product under weak Gaussian noise perturbation should be stated.

6) The bound appears to depend condition number of the covariance. If the covariance is not positive definite it appears the bound is non-sensical because the covariance is singular, the Gaussian distribution is degenerate, and the smallest eigenvalue is zero. The method and bound's dependence on the covariance should be clarified.  Starting with the fact that the calculation of von Neumann entropy has to deal with $0\cdot \log(0)=0$ when the output of the projection layer is less than the batch size. 

7) Theorem 5.1, a single $\Sigma$ is stated but the piecewise linearity would mean that the covariance depends on $X_2$. There is not a single covariance. That means that $\lamba_1$ and $\lambda_d$ depend on the input and it would seem. This seems to loosen the bound and the validated of this proof is questionable. 

8) In practice $\beta$ has to be picked. It doesn't appear the paper uses the theory to choose it.  The supplement states that it  must linearly scale from 1 to 10. Is this across epochs or the hyper-parameter search? How is this range selected? 

9) Figure 2 caption is not direct. Is this the same network with different metrics, or a different network for each metric?

10) I find it confusing/misleading that there is stated in the abstract that existing methods have a batch size dependence, but Figure 3 clearly shows a dependence on performance with batch size, albeit at smaller batch sizes than existing. 

11) A didn't find a thorough description of how hyper-parameter (batch size, learning rate) were chosen. I assume through validation set but only the selected ones are reported.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Update after the revision:
I thank the authors for the revision and engagement with my concerns as well as the other reviewers. I'd say that most of the revisions are all in the right direction. (The subsection "Quantum representation" in the discussion didn't actually offer much insight and seemed out of place at that point of the paper. It seems to me that the von Neumann entropy as an approach to encourage batch normalization to also yield disentangled (uncorrelated) representations would be a more concrete discussion.)

While some of my concerns have been addressed, item 4 and 7 above were not fixed. As item 7 was expanded in depth by reviewer heVY (whose more formal analysis was useful for everyone), and the authors concede that the theorem 5.1 is flawed,  I believe the paper is still lacking in aspects needed for acceptance at this time. The experimental results are promising but mixed. It seems that on some data sets it performs marginally better and on others it performs substantially worse than some existing methods. My concern is that there is no analysis (theoretical or experimental) that indicates why this would be the case. The experimental results show a reduction of variance in the updates, but how this translates to practice is unclear. 

Thus, although the paper sets out a new approach for framing self-supervised loss in terms of quantum (matrix based) information theory, the theory is not rigorously applied. Thus it is unclear how much the perspective actually helps, which decreases the contribution of the current version of the paper. I maintain my score of borderline reject.

===============
The paper is promising in both theory and results. However, there are some issues with the main presentation of von Neumann entropy in the finite sample case, as well as some unaddressed implications of singular covariances and other details. Addressing these issues along with some revision and reorganization will improve the clarity and logic of the paper, and I am willing to raise my score.

content.title: Authors' response
content.comment:
Thank you for your encouraging comments. We have addressed your comments as much as possible (we believe all have been addressed, but some were subtle issues), and please check the yellow and green highlights in the updated pdf. Additional responses are provided below. 

R1-#8: The hyperparameter $\beta$ is linearly increased from 1 to 10, and this information has been added to Appendix B (page 14). From our experiments, we have noticed that the von Neumann entropy term saturates faster than the cosine similarity term. Therefore, we decided to increase $\beta$ as the training is carried out. From our experience, however, the performance of learning is not sensitive to the choice of $\beta$ because both loss terms need to become small anyway.  
 
R1-#9: Same network, trained with 3 different losses. We have updated the caption. 

R1-#10: The batch size dependency is not any dependency, but the “dependency expressed as O(log(n))”. Our method is not dependent on O(log(n)). For additional details, please see the newly added discussion item of “Limitation of log(d)” in the discussion section.

R1-#11: We have adopted the hyperparameter settings from previous works, and therefore there was no need for tuning. For batch size and learning rate, the only description we have found for a small epoch value was in the SimSiam paper where they explain the hyperparameters used for reproducing 100-epoch BYOL results. We have blindly used the same learning rate setting in our experiments. For the momentum coefficient, we have used 0.9 because it is commonly adopted for imageNet training. This information has been updated on page 14.    

Also, please see our “General response to all reviewers”.

replying_to: Replying to Mutual Information Estimation as a Difference of Entropies for Unsupervised Representation Learning

content.title: General response to all reviewers:
content.comment:
We are truly grateful to receive your insightful and constructive comments. Overall, we fully agree with your main comments, and we have made the necessary revisions in the newly uploaded pdf. 

The following color coding was used for your convenience.    
- Multiple reviewers: highlighted in yellow
- Reviewer 1 (7tZk): highlighted in green
- Reviewer 2 (heVY): highlighted in orange
- Reviewer 3 (g1dt): highlighted in blue
- Reviewer 4 (6s5e): highlighted in pink

The main updates can be summarized as below.

* G-1: The title was updated.  
Indeed, we are not proposing a new mutual information estimator. In the original title, we wanted to say that “(we consider) *Mutual Information Estimation* (formulated) *as a Difference of Entropies* (and then we derive from the formulation a loss function that utilizes a von Neumann entropy bound) *for Unsupervised Representation Learning*”. We didn’t intend to say that we are deriving a new MI estimator. Somehow, however, we ended up saying “a new MI estimator” a few times in the main text. They were clearly our mistakes, and we have fixed the title and also all the clumsy writings in the main text. 
* G-2: The claim was adjusted. 
We have loosened our claims as recommended by the reviewers, and we have fixed the writings to be as conservative as possible. For instance, the word “principled” was deleted from six sentences and our method is never explained as “principled” anymore. Also, we never say “our mutual information estimator” anymore, and the tightness (or looseness) of our bounds is clearly discussed in “7. Discussion; Quantum representation”. 
* G-3: We moved Section 3.1 to Appendix A ("A brief introduction to quantum theory”).
* G-4: Using the space that we gained by deleting Section 3.1, we have added two items into the discussion section. In particular, we discuss “quantum representation” and its possible potential in deep learning. As a side note, our ultimate research goal is to understand the deep representation from the perspective of information theoretic coding theories, and this work was performed as a part of the effort. In this work, we were not able to learn quantum representation, but we believe our findings will be useful for the practical implementations of unsupervised learning (and hopefully also for making a micro step toward a better understanding of “deep representation”).
